idiom_name: guard value bound to scope exit (destructor / using / with / defer / try-finally)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare a guard at the top of the critical section whose creation acquires the lock and whose scope exit releases it, so that no exit path can skip the release. The release must be attached to the scope mechanism the language guarantees to run - a destructor (RAII), a using/with statement, a defer, or a try/finally - never to a path the programmer must remember. Keep exactly one guard per lock and keep the scope minimal; a guard that outlives the critical section, or a temporary that is destroyed immediately, silently changes the lock duration. When several locks must be held, acquire them through the platform's deadlock-avoiding multi-lock if one exists and document the ordering.
code_sketch:
guard = lock.acquire_scoped()        # acquire on scope entry
# --- critical section: shared-state operation only -------------
...
# --- scope exit releases the lock on every path, incl. exceptions
pitfalls: Emulations built on macros or hand-written try/finally reintroduce exactly the omission risk the pattern removes.
A guard created as a temporary, or copied/moved into a wider scope, releases at the wrong time.
Holding the guard across a blocking or awaiting operation extends the critical section and can deadlock.

The guard may outlive the mutex: destroying or moving the lock while a guard still references it (e.g. destroying the guarded object before the guard) makes the scope-exit unlock act on freed memory - std::scoped_lock documents this as undefined behaviour.

A movable or otherwise transferable guard lets the release happen on a thread other than the acquirer, which POSIX normal mutexes reject and Rust rules out by making MutexGuard !Send; only deliberately movable guard types may cross threads.

Hand-rolled guard classes are copyable by default, so a copy can double-unlock at scope exit or unlock a lock it never acquired; the standard guards delete copy construction exactly for this reason, and emulations must do the same.
